How a date gets into trouble

Sales needs a date

You take the estimate, add a margin and hope it's enough. Nobody can tell you how much margin is enough.

The status meeting is green

Your gut says otherwise. Nobody wants to be the first to say it, and without a number it sounds like you're covering yourself.

It slips, and you explain

The team did its usual month. The date moved anyway. You're the one in front of the client or your CEO.

How the number is made

Where a number like 34% comes from

Take the example at the top: 67 items, promised for March 15. If that team keeps finishing work the way it did in the last twelve weeks, it makes March 15 about one time in three.

I don't ask the team for a better estimate. I take what they finished in those twelve weeks, fast weeks and slow ones, and play the 67 items forward 10,000 times. 3,400 of those runs are done by March 15. That's the 34%. The realistic date is the one 8,500 runs made.

Why not a better estimate? I checked 880 software tasks with the same kind of work, the same estimate and the same process. Half were done within three days. One in twenty took longer than four weeks. There was no better estimate to find.

The Audit says where a date really lands and what to change. Both come from work I did inside a team.

Spotto: the promise I wouldn't make

Two months after launch, I was asked to commit to the quarter's plan: 14 items by 30 June, with at most 10% left undone. I said I couldn't promise it. 13 of the 14 were accepted eight days early. A forecast on that team's own record, run three years later, gave the plan an 86% chance of holding. The number I needed was already in our tracking history.

Before you start

Do you need our estimates or story points?

No. The forecast uses what your team finished and when, not what anyone estimated.

How is this different from the dashboard we already have?

A dashboard shows how work moves through your team today. The forecast tells you where you end up, for a date you've already promised to someone.

How do I know the number is right?

It isn't an opinion. It's your team's own last twelve weeks, played forward. The method and the data behind it are public, and running it again next month shows whether the date is getting closer.

Is the free Scan enough on its own?

If you can still move the date or cut scope, yes. You get the chance, the realistic date and how much of each closes the gap, and it's free to run again next month. When neither can move, the Delivery Audit starts from the same calculation and finds what is holding the date back, like finished work that waits days for a review.

What do you read from our tracker?

Status changes, created and resolved dates, and issue types. No titles, descriptions, comments or attachments, and not who did the work. The connection is read-only. Your data is only held in memory while the forecast runs. The result is kept 90 days, so you can share it. What is used, and what isn't →

We don't use Jira or Azure DevOps.

The free Scan connects to Jira Cloud and Azure DevOps. Working with another tracker like Linear? Tell me which one and we can find a solution.

Will you contact me afterwards?

No. No account, and nobody calls you. If you want to talk, you book it.

What if our tracker is a mess?

The Scan still runs. It counts an item as done on the day your tracker marks it resolved. If your releases come later than that, so does your real date. Checking what "done" means in your team is part of the Delivery Audit.

Start with your number.

Three minutes, read-only, no account. If the number is fine, you're done.

In short: Bart Pinnock tells software teams the chance that a promised date holds, from their own tracker history, and what to change to improve it. Independent, based in Ghent, Belgium. Works in Dutch or English.

For whom: CTOs and heads of engineering at software companies who promised a date to a client or to their CEO and are not sure it will hold.

How it works: no estimates or story points. The forecast takes what the team finished, plays the remaining work forward 10,000 times (a Monte Carlo simulation) and counts the runs that are done by the date. That share is the chance. The realistic date is the one 85 of 100 runs made. Method and data.

Start here: the free Delivery Scan. A tool the team runs itself: connect Jira Cloud or Azure DevOps read-only, pick a project and its deadline. In about three minutes it gives the chance of making the deadline, the realistic date, and how much later or how much scope cutting closes the gap. It uses the last twelve weeks. Free to run again. No account.

When the chance is low and the date can't move: the Delivery Audit, €4,500 excluding VAT. It starts with a detailed model of how work moves through the team. The same calculation as the Scan then runs on that model, for up to five deadlines, up to a year ahead.

The report gives the chance for each deadline, the main reasons a date may be missed, and a list of ways to improve the workflow, with a one-page summary for the CEO. Ready 14 days after a free 30 minute call. Four weeks later the same things are measured again.

Data: read-only. Status changes, created and resolved dates, issue types. No titles, descriptions, comments, attachments, or who did the work. Held in memory while the forecast runs. The result is kept 90 days.

Not a fit if: the question is what to build, not when it lands. You want Scrum or SAFe installed. You need someone in the delivery seat for six months.

In practice: at Spotto, a quarter plan Bart wouldn't promise landed eight days early. A forecast on that team's own record gave it an 86% chance. Work coming back after review or testing fell from 61% to 21%. At Factry, client implementation time went from 18 months to 6.
